name: Vision Transformer and Swin Transformer on Sentinel-2 patches

identity.method_name: Vision Transformer (ViT) and Swin Transformer applied to Sentinel-2 patches, from plain patch classification/segmentation through the current frontier of few-shot semantic segmentation with learnable prototypes (LPFS) and diffusion-inpainting-augmented few-shot segmentation (RS-Paint, arXiv:2503.03785)
identity.core_idea: ViT splits an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embeds each one, and applies global self-attention across all patches so every location can attend to every other location in one layer, in contrast to a CNN's local receptive field. Swin Transformer restores some of that locality and multi-scale structure by computing self-attention inside small shifted windows and merging patches hierarchically, which makes it more suitable than plain ViT for dense per-pixel prediction (segmentation) at moderate compute cost. The frontier extension, few-shot semantic segmentation, trains a meta-learning model on classes with abundant labels ('base classes') so that at test time it can segment a genuinely new class ('novel class', here: encroachment/water) from only 1-5 example masks ('shots'); LPFS does this with a VAE-based learnable-prototype module, and RS-Paint instead uses an image-conditioned diffusion inpainting model plus SAM to synthesise extra labelled novel-class examples before training an ordinary segmentation model on the enlarged set.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None specific to Bengaluru lakes. The transformer architectures themselves are not tied to a dataset. Benchmarks used in the literature reviewed here: iSAID-5i and LoveDA-2i (few-shot splits of iSAID and LoveDA, used to train/evaluate LPFS), ISPRS Potsdam, LoveDA, and DeepGlobe (used for RS-MTDF/related transformer-distillation work), and fMoW-Sentinel / BigEarthNet / EuroSAT (used for generic ViT/Swin-on-Sentinel-2 pretraining benchmarks). None of these is an official GEE/Kaggle catalog product; none targets lake water bodies or Bengaluru specifically.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: For plain supervised ViT/Swin training or fine-tuning: programmatic weak supervision from the existing MNDWI/NDVI rule, or a small hand-annotated set, exactly as for the U-Net item -- transformers do not remove this requirement and in fact need MORE labelled pixels than a CNN of comparable capacity to train stably from scratch, because they lack CNN's built-in spatial inductive bias. For the few-shot frontier (LPFS, RS-Paint): the proxy strategy shifts to transfer from another labelled dataset for the 'base classes' (e.g. pretrain/meta-train on iSAID or LoveDA, which have nothing to do with lakes) plus manual annotation for a handful of 'novel class' support examples (the encroachment/water class), typically 1-5 shots per episode. The manual support-set cost is small in absolute pixel count (a handful of hand-drawn masks) but is still real manual annotation, not zero-label learning, and it is still not real encroachment ground truth -- it is the student's own visual judgement of what 'encroached' looks like in a chip, encoded as a training mask.
fit_to_project.input_required: Multiband Sentinel-2 patches at a fixed spatial size (a ViT/Swin patch-embedding grid needs a consistent input resolution, e.g. 224x224 or 256x256 px). The project's cached B02, B03, B04, B08, B11, SCL bands at 20 m EPSG:32643 can supply this directly for a plain from-scratch ViT/Swin (no external pretrained-weight band contract to satisfy). LPFS and RS-Paint, however, are built and evaluated on 3-channel RGB (or RGB-equivalent very-high-resolution) imagery; using them on the project's 5-band 20 m multispectral stack would require either discarding B08/B11 (losing exactly the bands the current baseline depends on) or re-architecting their input embedding and retraining the base-class meta-training phase from scratch on multispectral data, which is a materially larger undertaking than the papers themselves describe.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed, and less favourably than for a CNN. Plain ViT/Swin trained from scratch is data-hungry -- these architectures are well documented to need larger training sets than CNNs to reach comparable accuracy, because they must learn positional/spatial structure that a CNN gets for free from convolutional weight-sharing. Reframed to patch/pixel level the same way as the U-Net item, the same ~6-lake spatial-block ceiling applies (see the U-Net item's analysis: effective n=6 lakes for any cross-lake generalisation claim, not 42 and not the pixel count). For the few-shot frontier specifically, the project's 6 lakes could in principle supply the 1-5 'shots' needed at inference time, since few-shot segmentation is explicitly designed for exactly this data regime -- but only after the (large, unrelated) base-class meta-training phase has already been done on an external dataset, which the project's 42 rows cannot supply on their own.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels for plain ViT/Swin (same as U-Net). For LPFS/RS-Paint: needs-weak-labels at the base-class level (external dataset, not a ground-truth problem for this project) plus a small amount of direct manual annotation for the novel-class support set, which is unavoidable in a few-shot segmentation formulation by design -- few-shot still means 'few labels', not 'zero labels'.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Plain ViT/Swin trained from scratch: yes, matches, because there is no inherited pretrained-resolution assumption (same argument as the from-scratch U-Net item). LPFS: pretrained/evaluated on iSAID (GSD not fixed, sub-metre to a few metres, satellite/aerial mix) and LoveDA (Chinese urban/rural land-cover, ~0.3-2 m aerial imagery) -- this IS the resolution mismatch the note asks to flag explicitly: a model meta-trained on sub-metre to few-metre aerial/VHR imagery is not validated at 20 m Sentinel-2 GSD, where a single pixel covers a 20x20 m area that could contain multiple mixed land-cover types the iSAID/LoveDA-trained prototype module has never seen at that scale. RS-Paint: built on 'Paint by Example' / Stable Diffusion inpainting, itself trained on natural RGB photographs and fine-tuned for RGB remote sensing scenes at typical diffusion-model resolutions (512x512 px, 3-channel) -- again a sub-metre/RGB-photograph resolution and channel assumption applied conceptually to 20 m 5-6 band reflectance data, a second clear instance of the resolution/domain mismatch this field is meant to catch.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: Plain ViT/Swin: weak/proxy labels (MNDWI/NDVI rule or manual), same as U-Net. LPFS/RS-Paint: external base-class dataset labels (iSAID, LoveDA, or similar, entirely unrelated to lakes) plus a handful of manually drawn novel-class support masks from the student.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the four stated limitations is fixed outright by choosing a transformer architecture instead of a CNN. (1) 42 rows: unaffected, and plain ViT/Swin's higher data appetite makes this limitation slightly WORSE, not better, relative to a CNN of similar capacity, unless a strong pretrained backbone is used (which pushes this item back toward A6's frozen-encoder territory). (2) static OpenStreetMap buildings: untouched, different data source. (3) no ground truth: not fixed; few-shot segmentation reduces the volume of labels needed but does not eliminate the need for the student's own manual judgement calls, which remain a proxy, not ground truth. (4) one dry-season scene per year: untouched; none of ViT, Swin, LPFS, or RS-Paint as reviewed here has a documented multi-temporal fusion mechanism for lakes (contrast with SatMAE/Prithvi/TerraMind in item A6, which do).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No, for the same structural reason as every single-scene image model reviewed in this study: neither a transformer's global attention nor a few-shot prototype can distinguish 'temporarily drained for maintenance' from 'permanently filled for construction' from one dry-season image alone, because the distinguishing evidence is temporal (does the water return?) and external (KTCDA desilting records), not visible in a single patch's spectral/textural content regardless of architecture.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: Speculatively better than the classical threshold for the same reason noted in item A6 (broader learned texture/context beats a hard NDVI cut in principle), but unverified: none of ViT/Swin-from-scratch, LPFS, or RS-Paint have been benchmarked on aquatic macrophyte/hyacinth classes. If a from-scratch Swin (which, unlike LPFS/RS-Paint, can natively ingest the project's full 5-6 band stack including NIR/SWIR) is trained with a dedicated hyacinth-vs-water-vs-vegetation weak-label scheme, it has a plausible shot at this confound; LPFS and RS-Paint, restricted to RGB-equivalent input, would lose the NIR/SWIR contrast the current baseline itself relies on to define the confound, making them structurally weaker on this specific point than either the plain-transformer or the U-Net/A6 options.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None. Like every other model reviewed in this study, ViT/Swin/LPFS/RS-Paint output a classification or segmentation mask over whatever polygon or patch is supplied; none references the Bengaluru Master Plan 30 m buffer, the earlier NGT 75 m buffer, KTCDA records, Survey of India records, Bhuvan, or the National Wetland Atlas 2024. Architecture choice does not change this field.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Same as the U-Net item: every one of the project's cached bands genuinely varies year to year, so no NEW static-snapshot problem is introduced. None of ViT, Swin, LPFS, or RS-Paint as reviewed here has a built-in multi-temporal mechanism (unlike SatMAE/Prithvi/TerraMind in A6), so this family gains nothing from, and loses nothing to, the single-scene-per-year limitation beyond what any single-frame image model already has.

implementation.libraries: Plain ViT/Swin from scratch or fine-tuned: PyTorch, timm (has both vit_* and swin_* model families), torchvision, segmentation-models-pytorch (for a Swin-UNet-style decoder), rasterio/geopandas for I/O. LPFS: no confirmed public code repository was located during this research; reproducing it would mean re-implementing the VAE-based learnable-prototype module described in the IEEE TGRS paper from scratch (PyTorch), on top of a chosen backbone and the iSAID/LoveDA few-shot splits, which is itself a nontrivial engineering task. RS-Paint: official code at github.com/SteveImmanuel/rs-paint, built on 'Paint by Example' (Stable Diffusion inpainting fork), plus Segment Anything Model (SAM, facebookresearch/segment-anything) for mask refinement, plus a separate off-the-shelf segmentation model (e.g. a U-Net or DeepLab) trained on the diffusion-augmented set.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Generic ImageNet-pretrained ViT-Base/Small and Swin-Tiny/Small/Base weights are widely available via timm/torchvision, all trained on 3-channel 224x224 natural RGB photographs -- adapting the first patch-embedding layer to the project's 5-6 band 20 m input is standard practice (as noted for the U-Net item) but dilutes the pretrained-weight benefit, since ImageNet features never saw Sentinel-2 spectral response curves. Satellite-domain-pretrained ViT/Swin weights exist mainly as the backbones already covered under item A6 (SSL4EO-S12's ViT-Small, SatMAE's ViT-Large, TerraMind's transformer backbone) -- using those here would collapse this item into A6's frozen-encoder approach rather than a genuinely separate from-scratch ViT/Swin item. LPFS: model weights are not confirmed to be publicly released alongside the IEEE TGRS paper [verify]. RS-Paint: relies on the publicly released 'Paint by Example' Stable-Diffusion-inpainting checkpoint (RGB, natural-image-pretrained) plus SAM's public ViT-H/L/B checkpoints (Apache-2.0), neither pretrained on satellite imagery.
implementation.licence: PyTorch/timm/torchvision/segmentation-models-pytorch: BSD/Apache-style, fully permissive, no restriction. SAM (facebookresearch/segment-anything): Apache-2.0, fully permissive. RS-Paint (github.com/SteveImmanuel/rs-paint): Apache-2.0, fully permissive. 'Paint by Example' base checkpoint: released under the CreativeML Open RAIL-M licence (the standard Stable-Diffusion-family licence), which is usable for academic research but carries content-use restrictions (no illegal/harmful generation) that should be disclosed, not a commercial blocker for this project but worth naming since the task requires licence verification before recommending anything [verify -- exact licence terms for the specific Paint-by-Example checkpoint RS-Paint depends on were not independently confirmed in this session]. LPFS: no code/weights repository confirmed, so no licence to evaluate; if the student re-implements it independently from the paper's method description, only the student's own code licence applies. iSAID/LoveDA/ISPRS Potsdam/DeepGlobe (base-class training data, if the student attempts to reproduce LPFS or RS-Paint's meta-training from scratch): each carries its own research-use terms and none includes India/Bengaluru imagery.
implementation.compute_requirement: Plain ViT/Swin trained from scratch on 42 lake-year patches: feasible on CPU only in the sense that the data volume is tiny, but transformers converge slowly and unstably on very small datasets without strong regularisation and data augmentation, so a free Colab/Kaggle T4 GPU session is strongly advisable for training turnaround even though it is not strictly impossible on a laptop CPU for a small Swin-Tiny model over many hours. LPFS: reproducing it from the paper's description would require full meta-training on iSAID-5i/LoveDA-2i (thousands of base-class images, multiple training episodes) -- this is a GPU-day-scale undertaking, well beyond a single free Colab session's 12-hour runtime limit in one sitting, and would likely need to be split across multiple sessions or use a smaller/lighter proxy dataset. RS-Paint: diffusion inpainting generation needs roughly 9 GB of GPU memory per 512x512 sample per the repository's own documentation -- this fits a free Colab T4 (16 GB) but not comfortably on a typical laptop CPU (diffusion sampling on CPU is extremely slow, many minutes per image), and generating enough synthetic novel-class examples to meaningfully augment a segmentation training set (tens to hundreds of samples) would consume a meaningful fraction of a free-tier GPU quota; the downstream segmentation-model training on the augmented set is comparatively cheap.
implementation.student_days: Plain ViT/Swin fine-tuned or trained from scratch for the project's own binary/4-class task: roughly 6-9 student-days (weak-label reuse from the U-Net pipeline if already built, 1; band-adapter and small-dataset regularisation tuning, 2-3; leave-one-lake-out training loop, 2; evaluation/writeup, 1-2) -- comparable to or slightly more than the U-Net item because of the extra regularisation tuning transformers need on small data. LPFS reproduced faithfully: unrealistic for one student in this project's timeframe -- honestly 15-25+ student-days including re-implementing the VAE prototype module (no confirmed public code), running meta-training on an external base-class dataset, and only then adapting to the 6-lake novel class; this exceeds what a single student with a laptop-plus-free-Colab budget can responsibly commit to alongside the rest of the capstone. RS-Paint adapted (not faithfully reproduced, since multispectral retraining of the diffusion model is out of scope): roughly 8-12 student-days if restricted to its native RGB pipeline (using only B04/B03/B02 and accepting the loss of B08/B11 information) to generate synthetic augmented RGB training chips for a separately trained small segmentation model -- still a large fraction of the project's total available time budget for a single sub-method.

evaluation.metrics: For plain ViT/Swin: same metrics as the U-Net item -- per-class F1/IoU, mean IoU, confusion matrix, and comparison of derived water/vegetation area against the classical baseline; accuracy alone is inadequate for the same class-imbalance reasons. For LPFS/RS-Paint few-shot evaluation: mean IoU over the novel class specifically (the standard few-shot segmentation metric, reported per shot count, e.g. 1-shot and 5-shot mIoU), which is more informative here than overall accuracy since the novel class (encroachment/water) is exactly the minority class of interest.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Leave-one-lake-out (6 folds) for plain ViT/Swin, identical justification to every other image-based item in this study. For LPFS/RS-Paint, the natural split is leave-one-lake-out at the SUPPORT-SET level: each lake in turn plays the role of the 'novel class' query, with support shots drawn from a different lake -- this is a stricter and more informative test than randomly sampling shots and queries from the same 6-lake pool, and should be used instead of within-lake shot/query splits, which would leak the same shoreline's appearance between support and query.
evaluation.leakage_risk: All the leakage risks already noted for the U-Net item apply identically here (spatial autocorrelation within a lake, pseudo-label circularity against the MNDWI/NDVI rule). An additional risk specific to the few-shot route: if the 'novel class' support shots and the evaluation queries are drawn from the SAME lake (even different years), the prototype/embedding can trivially match on shoreline geometry and sensor artefacts rather than a genuine encroachment signature, inflating apparent few-shot performance; this must be avoided by the leave-one-lake-out support/query split described above. For RS-Paint specifically, synthetic diffusion-generated training images that are conditioned on the project's own limited example set risk 'memorising and recombining' the same handful of real examples rather than generalising, which can look like successful augmentation while actually just re-presenting near-duplicates of the original few shots to the downstream segmentation model.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None of plain ViT/Swin, LPFS, or RS-Paint produce a calibrated uncertainty by default. As with every other item in this study, a defensible interval requires bootstrap resampling of the small evaluation set or Monte-Carlo-dropout/deep-ensemble wrapping, which is straightforward to add to a from-scratch ViT/Swin but has not been documented for LPFS or RS-Paint in their source papers.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Directly and materially applicable to RS-Paint, unlike any other item reviewed in this study group: RS-Paint's entire mechanism IS synthetic image generation (diffusion inpainting) to create additional novel-class training examples from a handful of real ones. If the small number of real Bengaluru-lake support examples the student manually labels are visually ambiguous or mis-judged (an inherent risk given there is no ground truth), the diffusion model will confidently generate MORE synthetic examples that amplify and entrench that same misjudgement, potentially fabricating a plausible-looking but false 'encroachment' pattern across the augmented set. This must be disclosed prominently and explicitly if RS-Paint's approach is used: every reported number derived from a model trained on diffusion-augmented data must state how many of the training examples were real versus synthetic, and any trend claim must be re-checked on the real examples alone before being reported as a finding.

evidence.published_performance: Swin-UNet on 10-category Sentinel-2 segmentation reports mean IoU 72.06% and accuracy 89.77% (MDPI Remote Sensing 2022, 'Multi-Category Segmentation of Sentinel-2 Images Based on the Swin UNet Method', doi 10.3390/rs14143382) [verify -- exact figures taken from a secondary summary, not independently re-derived from the paper's results table in this session]. LPFS ('Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation on Remote Sensing Images With Learnable Prototype', IEEE TGRS 2025, doi 10.1109/TIP.2026.3709522 or the IEEE Xplore document 10994816) reports 'significant performance improvements' on iSAID-5i and LoveDA-2i few-shot benchmarks over prior prototype-based baselines, but exact mIoU figures were not independently confirmed against the primary source in this session [verify]. RS-Paint (arXiv:2503.03785, ICLR ML4RS 2025 oral) reports that diffusion-generated synthetic novel-class samples 'significantly improve performance in low-data scenarios' for off-the-shelf segmentation models, but specific mIoU/accuracy delta numbers were not independently confirmed against the primary paper's tables in this session [verify].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Swin-UNet 10-category study: general Sentinel-2 10 m multi-class land cover, region and lake-water-hyacinth specifics not established from the sources reviewed [verify region]. LPFS: iSAID (sub-metre to few-metre satellite/aerial imagery, general object categories, no lakes) and LoveDA (Chinese urban/rural land cover, ~0.3-2 m aerial, no lakes or hyacinth). RS-Paint: unspecified remote-sensing base dataset per available sources, RGB imagery, no confirmed lake or Indian-subcontinent content [verify]. None of these three is a 20 m Sentinel-2, hyacinth-affected, seasonally-drained tropical urban lake study; none is a direct forecast for 6 Bengaluru lakes.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No. No published application of plain ViT/Swin-for-lakes, LPFS, or RS-Paint to Indian urban lakes or Bengaluru specifically was located during this research.
evidence.evidence_recency: The Swin-UNet 10-category paper (2022) predates the project's 2023-onward priority window and should be treated as an older architectural precedent, not frontier evidence. LPFS (2025, IEEE TGRS) and RS-Paint (March 2025, arXiv:2503.03785, ICLR ML4RS 2025) are both within the requested 2023-onward window and represent the genuine current frontier the note asks to cover.
evidence.primary_sources: RS-Paint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.03785 ; https://github.com/SteveImmanuel/rs-paint ; project page https://rspaint.steveimm.id/ . LPFS: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10994816 (paywalled; abstract and secondary summaries only accessible in this session). Swin-UNet Sentinel-2: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs14143382 . Swin Transformer (base architecture): Liu et al. 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14030 . ViT (base architecture): Dosovitskiy et al. 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929 . SAM: https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything . Hyacinth cross-check (as in item A6): Bareuther, Klinge & Buerkert (2020), Remote Sensing 12(22):3843, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12223843 .

risk.failure_modes: Plain ViT/Swin trained from scratch on 42 lake-years is likely to underperform or badly overfit relative to a CNN of similar capacity (U-Net item), because transformers lack CNN's convolutional spatial prior and typically need thousands of training images to reach comparable accuracy; on the smallest lake (Sankey Tank, ~310 total 20 m pixels) there is arguably not enough spatial extent for a Swin's windowed attention to operate meaningfully at all. LPFS cannot be honestly attempted end-to-end in this project's timeframe: it has no confirmed public code, its VAE-based prototype module would need re-implementation from a paper description, its meta-training needs a large unrelated base-class dataset, and it has never been validated at 20 m multispectral resolution -- attempting a faithful reproduction risks consuming the entire project's remaining time budget for an unvalidated result. RS-Paint's core mechanism is architecturally RGB-only; naively feeding it the project's NIR/SWIR-inclusive data is not possible without retraining the diffusion model's own patch/channel embedding, which is a far larger undertaking than the paper itself describes, so any adaptation is necessarily restricted to the 3 visible bands (B02/B03/B04), discarding exactly the spectral information (B08, B11) the project's own current MNDWI/NDVI method depends on.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask, for plain ViT/Swin, 'why use a data-hungry transformer instead of the CNN you already built for the U-Net item, on the same 42 rows?' -- the honest answer is architectural curiosity/comparison value only, not a clear expected accuracy gain on this data volume, and this should be stated plainly rather than oversold. For LPFS/RS-Paint, a panel will ask 'is this actually implemented, or is this a literature citation?' -- given the compute and engineering realism assessed above, the honest answer for a solo student on a laptop-plus-free-Colab budget is that a faithful reproduction of either is NOT realistically achievable inside this project, and presenting it as an implemented result rather than a surveyed frontier method would not survive scrutiny.
risk.honest_expectation: Plain ViT/Swin: a workable but not clearly superior alternative to the U-Net item on the exact same 42-row, 6-lake data, worth at most a brief architectural comparison rather than a separate primary deliverable, with a plausible null result ('no meaningful accuracy difference from the CNN baseline, as expected given the small dataset') being an entirely acceptable and likely outcome. LPFS: not achievable as a faithful implementation within this project's realistic time and compute budget; at most, a partial or heavily simplified prototype-matching idea could be borrowed conceptually (e.g. computing class prototypes from a handful of hand-picked example patches and using nearest-prototype distance as a weak feature) without claiming to have reproduced the paper. RS-Paint: technically runnable end-to-end with modest Colab GPU time using its published RGB pipeline and pretrained Paint-by-Example/SAM checkpoints, but only after accepting the loss of NIR/SWIR information central to the project's existing method, and the augmentation-honesty risk (see evaluation) makes any resulting 'improvement' number fragile and hard to defend without disclosing exactly how many training examples were synthetic.

verdict.recommended_rank: consider-with-reasons for a brief plain ViT/Swin comparison against the U-Net baseline (adopt-if-time only as a secondary architectural ablation, never as the project's single required deep-learning model given its higher data appetite on only 42 rows); reject LPFS as unreachable for one student on a laptop-plus-free-Colab budget in this project's timeframe -- no public code, large unrelated base-class meta-training requirement, and never validated at 20 m multispectral resolution; consider-with-reasons for RS-Paint specifically as a 'considered, with reasons' frontier item for the final report rather than an implemented method -- it is technically runnable on free Colab, but only via its native RGB pipeline, which discards the NIR/SWIR bands the project's own baseline depends on, and its core augmentation mechanism carries a material risk of fabricating a plausible but false encroachment trend from the project's own unavoidably subjective few manual labels.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We reviewed Vision Transformer and Swin Transformer approaches, including the current few-shot segmentation frontier (LPFS, diffusion-inpainting augmentation); a plain Swin/ViT is a reasonable but not clearly better architectural alternative to our CNN baseline on 42 rows, while LPFS is out of reach for a solo student's compute and code-availability constraints and diffusion-based few-shot augmentation is technically feasible on free Colab but is being reported as a considered frontier method with named risks, not as an implemented result, because it forces us off our multispectral bands and risks manufacturing a false trend from our own unverifiable manual labels.
